searchText: <@211091239112671234> > Triage discussion: is this block dropping really feasible? And maybe it would be easier to form an image of this by looking at the reorg events on the CL layer? Didn't understand this comment, could you expand a little, I feel I should be able to help here We were discussing the feasibility of dropping blocks due bad transactions. How large part of the network / attestators you'd have to control in order for it to be meaningful. By "bad transactions" do you mean invalid transactions that makes block invalid? Or it's bad in some other sense so the bad is not invalid according the protocol? Bad as in 'undesired', where someone tries to censor them Context: https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/26829 If I understand correctly, you need to outweight previous block that you want to reorg. That's a lot of attestations. But I'm pretty sure if there would be such mechanism in place - it would be an attack surface to malform transactions in a way that tricks the mechanism to re-org target blocks and steal MEV from it. oh, I seems misunderstood the re-orgs you meant, you just want to show warning and not act in case censoring is detected. anyone have a rough number for the size of historical blocks on the CL? hard to tell as no one is syncing from genesis these days, but my rought guess would be order of 100GB. This doesn't include the states that often are reconstructed for some blocks. So this is funny. If you have a mechanism that disables builders based on some patterns related to transactions, then an attacker may craft transactions that tricks this mechanism in a way that builders are always disabled. This is probably a desired attack.
